b: If you've ever set up a trust or updated an old one, you know how tiring it can be. Most of us want to shelve the binder and move on.

I'm not an estate-planning professional, but I've learned the signing isn't the finish line. A revocable trust controls only what it owns or what is directed to it, and a perfect document does little if your accounts never made it in. Year end, with statements arriving anyway, seems like a good time to check.

Retitling was the part that surprised me. Some institutions make it easy: an online form, upload the supporting documents, done. Others want a Medallion Signature Guarantee, which comes from a bank or broker, not a notary, or an in-person meeting. It can be a pain. Don't let it stop you.
Bank, credit union and brokerage accounts, retitled to the trust or with a payable-on-death or transfer-on-death designation naming it, whichever your attorney intended.
Accounts and CDs opened since you signed. These are easy to miss.

Real estate. Was the deed actually recorded? Does your insurer know the trust holds title? Property in another state deserves special attention, since a second probate is often what the trust was meant to avoid.
A payable-on-death or transfer-on-death designation only works at death. If you become incapacitated, your successor trustee can't manage that account.
Accounts that pass by beneficiary form
IRAs and 401(k)s can't be retitled to a living trust; moving one there generally counts as cashing it out. What matters is the beneficiary form on:
Traditional, Roth and inherited IRAs, 401(k)s and 403(b)s, including plans at former employers.
HSAs, and the successor owner of any 529 plan.

Naming your spouse, children or trust on an IRA is a real decision, not paperwork. A spouse named directly can generally treat the IRA as their own, which a trust usually can't offer. The trust's wording affects how fast the money must come out, and income kept in a trust reaches the top federal bracket surprisingly quickly. This is one for the attorney.
What your trust says doesn't override these forms. Check the primary and contingent beneficiaries the institution actually has on file, not the ones you remember.
A pour-over will, which catches leftover assets but doesn't necessarily avoid probate.
A durable financial power of attorney, for anything outside the trust if you become incapacitated.
A health care directive and HIPAA authorization.
Are your successor trustees, executor and agents still the people you'd choose, and still willing and able to serve?
Do they know where your documents are and how to reach your attorney and accountant?
Is there a list of your accounts and policies they can find? Balances aren't needed.
Can someone securely reach your digital records and online accounts?

Families change too. Marriages, divorces, deaths and new grandchildren can all change what we intended. What made sense ten years ago may not today. I'm putting a reminder on next year's calendar, since every new account or rollover is another chance for something to slip through.
Most of this is housekeeping we can do ourselves. When something looks wrong, at least we know what to ask our attorney.
What did I leave off? If you've been through this, I'd like to hear what you check that isn't on this list.
